figures.claim: 2. Figure 2: Educational attainment shows no significant association with cognitive profile heterogeneity across diverse cognitive domains. Box plots reveal similar distributions of cognitive profile heterogeneity across all education levels, with overlapping interquartile ranges and comparable medians. Multiple linear regression with age, gender, country, and time-of-day covariates revealed no significant associations between education level and either heterogeneity metric after Bonferroni correction (alpha = 0.025). Education levels: Some HS (n=9), HS/GED (n=95), Some College (n=308), Associate's (n=240), College (n=396), Master's (n=173), Professional (n=80), Ph.D. (n=22). Sample: 1,083 participants from NeuroCognitive Performance Test Battery 26.
figures.explanation: Analysis stage: The per-education-level sample sizes in the figure caption conflict with the execution log (step4_output.txt). The log shows: edu1=9, edu2=95, edu3=240, edu4=396, edu5=63, edu6=190, edu7=22, edu8=68 (total=1083). The paper claims: Some HS=9, HS/GED=95, Some College=308, Associate's=240, College=396, Master's=173, Professional=80, Ph.D.=22 (total=1323 ≠ 1083). The reported per-group sizes for Some College (308 vs 240), Associate's (240 vs 63), Master's (173 vs 190), Professional (80 vs 22), and Ph.D. (22 vs 68) are all wrong; many appear shifted or swapped. The claimed total (1,323) also contradicts the stated sample of 1,083.

figures.claim: 1. Figure 1: Cognitive profile heterogeneity metrics demonstrate discriminant validity and distinct distributional properties independent of general cognitive ability. Both heterogeneity metrics show minimal correlation with overall cognitive performance, confirming they capture cognitive profile differentiation rather than general ability level. Panels A and B reveal that Percentile Range (r = 0.012, p = 0.691) and Percentile IQR (r = 0.063, p = 0.037) correlate weakly with the Grand Index composite score, with both correlations falling well below the |r| < 0.20 discriminant validity threshold. Panel C demonstrates that Percentile Range exhibits a broader distribution with higher mean values compared to Percentile IQR. Percentile Range: mean = 74.64, SD = 13.67; Percentile IQR: mean = 34.06, SD = 11.60; n = 1,083 participants from NeuroCognitive Performance Test Battery 26.
figures.explanation: Analysis stage: Step3 execution log shows: r=0.0121, p=0.6905 (range-grand_index); r=0.0633, p=0.0374 (IQR-grand_index); Range mean=74.643, SD=13.665; IQR mean=34.059, SD=11.603; n=1083. All match claimed values within rounding. The underlying data is in step3_heterogeneity_metrics CSV and step3_validation_results CSV.

figures.claim: 3. Figure 3: Educational attainment shows no differential relationship with cognitive profile heterogeneity across age groups. Age-stratified analysis reveals consistent patterns in the relationship between educational level and cognitive heterogeneity, contradicting predictions of cumulative differentiation effects in older adults. The absence of significant interaction effects (p > 0.025, Bonferroni-corrected) indicates that educational experiences do not produce stronger cognitive specialization patterns with extended exposure over the lifespan. Panel A shows younger adults (ages 18-39, N=530); Panel B displays older adults (ages 50+, N=383). Middle-aged adults (40-49, N=170) were included in statistical analyses but not displayed separately.
figures.explanation: Analysis stage: Step5 execution log confirms age group sizes: Younger=530, Older=383, Middle=170. All interaction terms were non-significant after Bonferroni correction (step5_output.txt: 'No significant interaction terms found after Bonferroni correction'). N values match claim exactly.

figures.claim: 4. Figure 4: Sensitivity analyses confirm the absence of educational effects on cognitive profile heterogeneity across multiple analytical approaches and metric definitions. Alternative heterogeneity metrics and analytical strategies yielded consistent null findings, reinforcing the robustness of the primary results. The coefficient of variation metric (Panel A) showed no systematic relationship with educational attainment. Collapsed education groupings (Panel B) revealed overlapping distributions with minimal between-group differences. Split-half reliability analyses (Panels C and D) demonstrated adequate internal consistency of heterogeneity metrics. Sample size n = 1,083 participants across all panels.
figures.explanation: Execution stage: The claim states Panels C and D 'demonstrated adequate internal consistency of heterogeneity metrics,' but the actual split-half reliability values are r=0.009 (range) and r=-0.032 (IQR) — effectively zero correlation, indicating no internal consistency. Standard psychometric thresholds require r>0.7 for adequate reliability. These near-zero values contradict the 'adequate internal consistency' characterization. Additionally, the overall CoV model (Panel A) shows F=1.926, p=0.001 (significant), conflicting with the 'null findings' framing, although individual education coefficients are non-significant. Panel B (collapsed education) results are genuinely null and consistent with the description.
figures.evidence: step6 split-half reliability: range r=0.0089 (p=0.770), IQR r=-0.0324 (p=0.286) — near-zero correlations. CoV regression: individual education coefficients all non-significant (p=0.156–0.837) but overall model F=1.926, p=0.001. Collapsed education (Panel B): F=0.738, p=0.846 (null). N=1,083 confirmed. | Code: agents4science_supp_materials/analysis/script_execution_logs/step_6_output.txt:683-684 (split-half r values); figure_4.py:121-177 (Panel C/D implementation)

results_section.claim: 13. An alternative coefficient-of-variation metric produced convergent null results, with very small explained variance (R2 = 0.0261; adjusted R2 = -0.0064) and a non-significant omnibus test (F = 0.8029, p = 0.7869)
results_section.explanation: Analysis stage: The step6 execution log shows the CoV regression used a fundamentally different model formula ('coefficient_of_variation ~ C(education_level, Treatment(1)) + age + C(gender) + C(country) + C(time_of_day)') with individual time_of_day levels (24 categories, Df Model=35) rather than binned time_of_day (4 categories) as in the primary models. The actual executed result is R²=0.060, Adj. R²=0.029, F=1.926, p=0.001, which is (a) a statistically SIGNIFICANT finding (p=0.001 < 0.05) and (b) entirely different from the paper's claims (R²=0.0261, F=0.8029, p=0.7869). The paper falsely characterizes a significant omnibus result as a null finding.
